Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA cor. Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dilg.gov.ph OPINION NO. S. 2014. HON. IRVING B. DASAYON Municipal Mayor Pinukpuk, Province of Kalinga Dear Mayor Dasayon: This has reference to the Sangguniang Bayan Resolution No. 100 series of 2023, requesting this Department's opinion on the propriety of crafting an ordinance granting honoraria to barangay senior citizen chapter presidents, secretaries, and treasurers of the 23 barangays of Pinukpuk, Kalinga. As premised, the passage of the subject Resolution was impelled by the letter of the Municipal Social Welfare and Development Officer, requesting the crafting of the said ordinance. The intent is to compensate for the travel expenses and meal allowance of said senior citizen-officers in planning, implementing, and monitoring compliance with their programs, projects, and activities and in assisting the senior citizen- members in their respective barangays in pursuance of the objectives of Republic Act No. 9994. At the outset, we note that Republic Act (RA) No. 99941, as amended, provides benefits and privileges to senior citizens. The said Act, however, does not expressly provide honoraria to senior citizens chapter officials, such as barangay senior citizens chapter presidents, secretaries, and treasurers. What is categorically provided is the grant of honorarium to the head of the Office of Senior Citizens Affairs (OSCA) from the city govemment. Section 6 of RA 9994, as amended, explicitly provides: "Section 6. xxx The head of the OSCA shall be entitled to receive an honorarium of an amount at least equivalent to Salary Grade IO to be approved by the LGU concerned." While local government units have the power to enact ordinances for the general welfare of their respective constituents, such power is not without limitations. The enactment of local ordinances should not be inconsistent with existing laws and regulations. Along this line, it is to be noted that the grant of honoraria is subject to certain limitations, such as the general principles of budgeting, the availability of funds, and other pertinent guidelines issued by competent authorities, such as the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) and the Commission on Audit (COA). At this juncture, it may be well to revisit what honorarium is. In Santiago v. COA (G.R. No. 92284, July 12, 1991), the Supreme Court defines "honorarium" as something given not as a matter of obligation but in appreciation for services rendered by a voluntary donation in consideration of services that admit no compensation in money. I "Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010." "Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan"

Pertinently, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) Local Budget Circular No. 622, specifically, Item 2. I thereof, provides that honorarium is "a form of compensation paid to a government official or employee for services rendered in addition to, but nevertheless form part of, his regular duties and responsibilities." Notably, the Supreme Court's definition of "honorarium" underscores the voluntary, appreciative or honorary nature of the honorarium, which implies that honorarium may not necessarily involve monetary compensation. On the other hand, the afore-cited DBM Circular emphasizes the compensatory aspect in which the government official or employee, whichever the case may be, is granted honorarium for doing extra services or tasks beyond their usual or regular duties. At any rate, a thorough perusal of the aforementioned DBM Circular reveals, though seemingly plain, that it inherently comprises two indispensable elements that must be considered to determine whether the grant of honorarium is warranted: (1) it should be paid to a qovernment official or employee for services rendered; and (2) the tasks or services rendered by the official or employee. as the case may be. are beyond his or her reqular duties; in other words. extra or additional services rendered. In DILG Legal Opinion No. 8, Series of 2019, we opined—premised on the aforesaid DBM Circular—that an honorarium can only be availed of by local government officials and employees performing or discharging duties in local govemment activities or special projects in addition to or over and above their regular functions, regardless of the source of funds. In the present case, it appears that the tasks or services, as stated in the subject Resolution—i.e. planning, implementing, and monitoring compliance of senior citizen programs, projects, and activities, and assisting senior citizen members in their respective barangays—do not fall within the contemplation of the aforecited DBM guidelines. Accordingly, the subject query should be answered in the negative. This opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities or the courts. We hope to have guided you accordingly. Ve truly yours, By the thority of the tary: JUAN VICTOR R. LLAMAS U rsecretary for External, Legal and Legislative Affairs O ELL_NJVRULLLS-LRALLD0am Dir.
